# Pruning fruit trees

Pruning fruit trees in late winter, while the trees are still dormant,
gives new growth the best possible start once spring arrives. Remove any
branches that are dead, damaged, or crossing another branch, and always
cut just above an outward-facing bud so new growth spreads away from the
center of the tree rather than crowding it.

Start with the largest structural cuts first: pick three to five main
scaffold branches that are evenly spaced around the trunk, and remove
competing leaders so the tree keeps a single strong central stem or an
open vase shape, whichever suits the species. Apples and pears generally
prefer a modified central leader; stone fruits like peaches and plums are
usually trained to an open vase so light reaches the interior.

Sanitize pruning tools between trees, especially when disease is a
concern, using a diluted bleach solution or rubbing alcohol wiped across
the blades. A dull or dirty blade tears bark instead of cutting cleanly,
and a ragged wound is slower to heal and more likely to invite pests or
fungal infection over the following season.

Water sprouts and root suckers should be removed as they appear through
the growing season rather than saved for the next dormant pruning, since
they crowd the canopy with weak, unproductive growth that shades out the
fruiting wood lower down. Thin the fruit itself in early summer if a
heavy fruit set threatens to break branches or produce a lot of small,
poorly flavored fruit at harvest.

Keep a simple record of what was cut each year, because a tree pruned
too hard in one season often responds with a flush of vigorous, upright
water sprouts the next season that then need their own attention, and
tracking the pattern over several years makes the whole job faster and
more confident.
